title: Usability Evaluation for High-Consequence Products
summary: This capability covers formative evaluation for complex products where interface failures can affect safety, operational continuity, clinical work, expert judgement, or commercial viability. It uses representative users, realistic task scenarios, abnormal scenarios, controlled comparisons, field observation, eye tracking, expert review and production deployment measurement where those methods are appropriate to the question being answered.
keyFacts: Formative evaluation identifies and addresses usability problems during design; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility in regulated medical contexts.
IEC 62366-1 governed evaluation requires participant selection, task design and documentation appropriate to the standard.
Representative users in expert tools means domain experts, not general users.
High-consequence evaluations must include abnormal conditions and non-happy paths because failures have consequences in those conditions.
The Torqeedo maritime HMI evaluation included 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains in actual maritime conditions.
The Torqeedo programme combined sea trial observation, a controlled experiment with 24 subjects and operational sea-trial eye tracking with 7 subjects.
The Kardion MCS Controller engagement built on an Emergo by UL formative study with 7 participants and 8 clinical use scenarios under IEC 62366-1.
The Squaremind evaluation used an ecological protocol with 29 users across London and Paris, age stratification and an independent dermatologist co-conducting sessions.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing used the production product installed in a car with 32 participants across two sessions, with three unassisted tasks per participant.
The maritime traffic software portfolio study published its own threats-to-validity table and refused significance tests, confidence intervals, power calculation and aggregation of timed percentages.

bodySections.heading: Definition and Scope
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Usability evaluation for high-consequence products is the structured formative evaluation of interfaces, workflows and system behaviour under realistic conditions. It uses representative users, realistic task scenarios and calibrated evidence methods to identify design problems before summative validation or deployment.

The evaluation question is not only whether users can complete ideal tasks. The question is whether representative users can interpret system state, recover from confusion, act under pressure and complete realistic task scenarios when conditions are non-ideal.

bodySections.heading: When High-Consequence Usability Evaluation Is Needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence usability evaluation is needed when ordinary usability testing would miss the conditions that expose interface failure. These conditions can include abnormal scenarios, divided attention, time pressure, expert decision-making, gloved interaction, glare, vibration, low bandwidth, mixed device fleets, live operational constraints and multi-role clinical or industrial choreography.

Representative users are part of the evaluation definition. In IEC 62366-1 language, participants must represent the intended user population. In expert tools, this means domain experts rather than general users.

High-consequence evaluation also requires abnormal scenario evaluation. Products used in maritime, clinical, industrial, automotive, customs, dermatology, aviation-related and process-control contexts do not fail only in happy paths. Evaluation therefore needs to include non-happy paths, abnormal conditions and situations where the performance difference between good and poor interfaces becomes visible.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Methods Used for Realistic Evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy structures usability evaluation around the question the evidence must answer. A controlled experiment can quantify a performance difference. Field observation can reveal conditions that a laboratory cannot reproduce. Eye tracking can measure visual attention during real tasks. Expert review can assess interface structure against domain knowledge. Production deployment measurement can show what happened in live operational use.

Creative Navy uses triangulation across evidence sources when a single method cannot answer all evaluation questions. Sea trial observation, controlled experiments, eye tracking, expert review, ecological testing, counterbalanced comparison, acceptance checks and production deployment measurement each answer different questions and carry different limitations.

The appropriate method depends on the product, the operational setting and the claim being tested. A prototype comparison, a formative IEC 62366-1 study, an ecological pre-deployment test and client-measured production data do not support the same conclusions.

bodySections.heading: What High-Consequence Usability Evaluation Produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence usability evaluation produces calibrated evidence rather than a single generic usability score. The output may be a list of design failures, a measured comparison, a design backlog, a set of acceptance checks, a formative evidence package or production deployment outcome data.

For interface design work, the evaluation output is useful only if the finding can be acted on. Creative Navy therefore treats evidence as design input: the finding must identify the behaviour observed, the condition that produced it, the consequence for the user or system, and the design decision it should affect.

In high-consequence contexts, a self-correction, a hesitation, an incorrect first response or a recovery after confusion may still be a finding. The point of formative evaluation is not to convert every eventual completion into success, but to identify where the interface creates avoidable risk, delay, cognitive load or ambiguity.

bodySections.heading: IEC 62366-1 Medical-Device Evaluation Boundaries
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's role in regulated medical usability evaluation is formative only. Summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility through the regulatory submission.

This distinction matters because formative evaluation supports design decisions and usability engineering evidence, while summative validation formally demonstrates regulatory compliance on a finalised design. IEC 62366-1 governed evaluation requires participant selection, task design and documentation appropriate to the standard.

Regulatory outcomes must be interpreted carefully. A submitted design passing regulatory evaluation is not the same as a measured clinical outcome, a safety result or a direct measurement of clinical performance.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Calibration and Interpretation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence usability evaluation does not automatically establish safety, clinical performance, operational performance over time or regulatory compliance. Each engagement establishes only what its protocol and evidence basis can support.

Evidence from a controlled experiment, a field observation, a prototype bench test, a design-conformance check, a client-run usability test and a production deployment measurement has different inferential strength. Creative Navy preserves those distinctions rather than compressing all results into broad claims about usability improvement.

Client-measured or client-reported results are treated differently from Creative Navy-recorded measurements. Prototype findings are treated differently from deployed-system findings. Design review feedback is treated differently from post-deployment evaluation. These boundaries are necessary because high-consequence products require evidence that remains accurate when reused in design, governance or regulatory discussion.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Creative Navy's role in regulated medical usability evaluation is formative only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.

The Torqeedo maritime HMI evaluation combined 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, a controlled experiment with 24 subjects and eye tracking with 7 subjects during actual sea trials.

The Kardion MCS Controller engagement built on an Emergo by UL formative study with 7 participants and 8 clinical use scenarios under IEC 62366-1, then used Creative Navy sessions with cardiologists and nurses to surface clinical choreography.
The Kardion submitted design passed FDA evaluation as submitted with no design changes required, recorded as FDA approval.
The Squaremind ecological evaluation recorded 27 of 29 patients completing the scan independently, with 12 users getting stuck and all 12 recovering without external intervention in 2–4 minutes.
Beissbarth production deployment data recorded calibration time changing from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 deployment locations.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing used the actual production product installed in a car; all 32 participants completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations.
Schone Airspace Group Mission Control first-candidate checks produced 14 pass, 18 fail and 4 pending results, while integrated retest produced 32 pass, 0 fail and 4 pending.
The maritime traffic software portfolio study used a formative round and a separate within-participant counterbalanced comparative round, and published explicit threats to validity.
weakerClaims: The industrial process-control rating is client-reported, based on a client-run 12-participant usability test of designs, and captures rated impressions rather than measured task performance.
limitations: Formative evaluation in regulated medical contexts is not summative validation; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.
Regulatory outcomes such as FDA approval are not measured usability outcomes or clinical performance measurements.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing validated comprehension of a finished design in a parked car, not long-term product use or safety.
Raymarine findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype bench fixture, with no field conditions, no live transmission and no significance testing.
Schone Airspace Group Mission Control pass figures are design-conformance results, not task completion rates, error rates, satisfaction scores or flight performance measures.
The maritime traffic software portfolio comparison bought within-participant attribution but cost external validity because the compared interfaces differed in more than the variable under test.
Beissbarth and Gexcon production deployment measurements were client-measured, and the exact repeated-measurements figure for Beissbarth is not available.
The industrial process-control 12-participant rating is client-reported, client-run, impression-based and conducted on designs rather than a deployed system.
Design review feedback from deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgeons is not post-deployment evaluation.
